document.text:

It's a two-story classic, stucco outside, with four bedrooms, three baths, and a little over twenty-five hundred square feet spread across a big half-acre-plus lot. Inside there's a fireplace in the living room, a formal dining room, and up top a wide rooftop deck where you can imagine catching the last of the evening light. Out back, patios wind between the plantings — room to garden, to gather, to simply breathe.

By 2025 it was ready for its next chapter. Listed with real vintage charm and great bones, though wanting some updates, it came onto the market and, after about five weeks, sold this past October for one point one million dollars — roughly four hundred and twenty-eight dollars a square foot.

A rare find, and a fresh start.

locating.anchor: the steep bare island glowing rusty red in the water

document.text: That steep, bare island rising from the bay has a secret: it is the only privately owned island in all of San Francisco Bay. Red Rock covers barely six acres, yet the borders of Marin, Contra Costa, and San Francisco counties all meet on it. Over the years its owners have dreamed up a casino, a twenty-story hotel, even a Playboy Club for this lonely outcrop — and in the nineteen eighties the guru Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh nearly bought it before his Oregon commune collapsed. One buyer paid just under fifty thousand dollars for it in nineteen sixty-four. In twenty twenty-three it was listed for twenty-five million, and a mystery buyer quietly scooped it up the following year. Through it all, nobody has ever really built anything here. The rock still glows rusty red from its iron-rich stone, and the bay keeps its one private island beautifully empty.

spot.title: Seadrift and the Sandspit
spot.subtitle: A seawall, a lawsuit, and a beach

locating.anchor: the long sandspit of beach houses across the water

document.text: Across the water, a long ribbon of beach houses rides the sandspit that shelters this entire lagoon. That is Seadrift, laid out by the William Kent Estate Company in the late nineteen forties. The pioneering city planner Catherine Bauer wrote its protective covenants in nineteen forty-nine, and the firm of architect William Wurster designed many of its early houses. It also became the stage for one of California's long-running beach-access fights. During the storms of nineteen eighty-three, homeowners built a rock seawall well over a mile long under an emergency permit, and the question of what the public was owed in exchange spent years in the courts. A settlement in nineteen ninety-four confirmed the public's right to walk Seadrift's ocean beach — though no closer than sixty feet from the seawall, with no camping or picnicking. The sandspit itself does quiet, essential work: it is the natural barrier that makes the lagoon a lagoon.

spot.title: Marin's Last Bargain
spot.subtitle: The sub-million-dollar corner of a three-million-dollar county

locating.anchor: the redwood grove where the creek runs close to the road

document.text: By Marin County standards, you are driving through a bargain. These wooded hamlets — Forest Knolls, Lagunitas, and their neighbors — are among the last places in the county where a typical home still trades under a million dollars. Redfin's market data put Woodacre's median sale price around eight hundred ninety-five thousand dollars at the end of twenty twenty-five, down more than seventeen percent from the year before, and recent medians for the Lagunitas and Forest Knolls market hover just above nine hundred thousand. Cross the ridge to Stinson Beach, where Zillow valued the typical home around three point seven million dollars in twenty twenty-four, and the same money buys a fraction of a house. The gap has a history: septic systems, fire danger, narrow roads, and decades of slow-growth politics kept this valley rustic while the rest of Marin turned into an asset class. Under the redwoods, cheap is relative — and it is disappearing.

spot.title: Victory Village
spot.subtitle: In a county famous for saying no to housing, Fairfax built fifty-four homes for seniors

locating.anchor: the newer apartment complex set back from Sir Francis Drake Boulevard near Oak Manor

document.text: Marin County is nationally famous for fighting new housing — which is what makes this building news. Victory Village opened here in the summer of twenty twenty: fifty-four affordable homes for seniors aged sixty-two and older, about a mile from downtown Fairfax. Eleven of the apartments were set aside for people coming out of homelessness, including six for residents living with serious mental illness. Twenty-eight units were designed for people with mobility impairments. Every household received a project-based rental subsidy, capping rent at thirty percent of income — in a county where market rents had pushed out a generation of elders on fixed incomes. The nonprofit Resources for Community Development shepherded the project through years of planning, funding rounds, and public meetings before crews finally broke ground. When the waiting list opened in February of twenty twenty, applications poured in — a measure of how many longtime Ross Valley residents were one rent increase away from leaving for good.

spot.title: Splitting the Town
spot.subtitle: The nineteen sixty-seven shopping center San Anselmo fought over — and needed

locating.anchor: the Safeway storefront anchoring Red Hill Shopping Center

document.text: When Sunny Hills finally closed its farm in nineteen sixty-three, the pasture at the foot of Red Hill became the most argued-over ground in town. Developers wanted a shopping center. Plenty of residents wanted no such thing. People said it would split the town in half, a slab of parking and storefronts dropped into the middle of a place that thought of itself as one long main street. But San Anselmo was a town of homes with almost no sales tax base, and in the end the arithmetic won. Red Hill Shopping Center opened in nineteen sixty-seven, anchored by a Safeway and a Longs drug store, while road crews spent that same decade rebuilding Sir Francis Drake and the Hub crossing to carry all the new traffic. The quarrel faded slowly into habit, and the center has been debated, replanned, and remodeled ever since. Still, the town got the tax receipts it badly needed, and the valley got its daily errands, groceries and prescriptions and hardware, sold from shelves standing on ground that was farm pasture within living memory, at the foot of the orphans' sunny hill.

spot.title: Villa Sites, Twenty-Five Cents a Ride
spot.subtitle: The railroad invents the Marin commuter dream at Sunnyside

locating.anchor: the Bolinas Avenue corner below the seminary hill, the last blocks of San Anselmo before Ross

document.text: These are the blocks of Sunnyside, a modest name for San Anselmo's oldest subdivision, first mapped in eighteen eighty-one when nearly everything around you was hayfield. The railroad had land along its line and seats to fill, so it turned salesman. Advertisements for these homesites hung in its stations and in the cabins of the ferryboats, and the company ran twenty-five cent round-trip excursions from San Francisco, rolling prospective buyers right past the lots. San Francisco auctioneers Easton, Eldridge and Company cried the bidding, moving about fifty so-called villa sites between eighteen eighty-seven and eighteen ninety. Sales crawled at first; the commuter dream needed better trains. But once the electric interurbans began racing to the ferry slips every half hour, the villa sites filled in with year-round houses, and the trains stopped at Bolinas Avenue here, the last San Anselmo station before Ross. Stand back and squint, and you can see what was invented on this ground: buy a cottage in the country, keep your job in the city, and let the railroad, and later the boulevard you are driving, carry you between your two lives. Half of Marin still lives by that bargain.

locating.anchor: at 300 Bothin Road

document.text: Three hundred Bothin Road contains a surprise that a street address cannot communicate: the public property record reproduced by Redfin describes a lot of about seventeen and a half acres. The house itself is listed at roughly twenty-three hundred square feet, with a construction date of nineteen thirty-seven. Those are two completely different scales of real estate, compressed into a single address. The recorded sale on July ninth, twenty nineteen, was two and a half million dollars. That is a historical transaction, not a current valuation. Now picture how misleading it would be to divide that whole purchase price by the indoor floor area and call the answer the price of building a house. The transaction included the land as well. A kitchen and a hillside are being squeezed into the same arithmetic. Nor does acreage tell us how much ground is level, accessible, or available for another building. The listing is a starting point for questions, rather than a map of development possibilities. This is one of the pleasures of walking Bothin: an ordinary-looking house number can conceal a property whose boundaries operate at the scale of a landscape.

spot.subtitle: Reading the dates at 180 Bothin Road

document.text: One hundred eighty Bothin Road offers a useful little detective story about real-estate numbers. Then the address appears again: listed in September of twenty twenty-four at one million seven hundred forty-five thousand, and withdrawn that November. A further listing in March of twenty twenty-five began at one million seven hundred twenty-five thousand. It was later withdrawn at a lower asking price. Notice what the record does not say: those later asking prices did not become recorded sales in that history. An advertisement is a proposal. A closing is an event. Mixing them up can make a neighborhood seem to appreciate simply because someone changed a number on a website. Here the better first question is: what happened, and when?

spot.title: A Midcentury House Learns New Tricks
spot.subtitle: Expansion and daylight at 112 Bothin Road

locating.anchor: at 112 Bothin Road

document.text: A construction date can make a house sound frozen in time. One hundred twelve Bothin Road shows why that is a mistake. Public listing records date the original house to nineteen fifty-nine, but the twenty twenty-five sale description presents an expanded and updated home, with five bedrooms in a little over twenty-one hundred square feet. The advertisement describes three bedrooms downstairs, additional bedrooms upstairs, skylights, and sliding doors linking the living spaces with outdoors. These are details from the sale materials, not things you need to see through anybody's windows. What interests me is the design problem: how do you add capacity while keeping the light and outdoor connections that made the original house appealing? An extra floor can preserve ground for a garden, while openings in the roof bring daylight into rooms that would otherwise depend on the edges of the building. This particular home sold on October twentieth, twenty twenty-five, for one million seven hundred eighty-two thousand five hundred dollars. But its longer story is architectural adaptation. A neighborhood can gain rooms, change its family arrangements, and update its buildings without replacing every old house with an entirely new one.

spot.title: The Flat Front and the Steep Back
spot.subtitle: What a carport application reveals at 131 Bothin

locating.anchor: at 131 Bothin Road

document.text: A modest remodeling application can reveal more about a property than a glossy listing. In May of twenty twenty-five, Fairfax planners examined a proposal at one hundred thirty-one Bothin Road: remodel the lower floor, add a bathroom, and build a two-car carport with a covered walkway. The surprise was the land. Staff described the frontage around the house as mostly flat, while the ground behind climbed steeply toward Iron Springs Road. The parcel's average slope was about thirty-six percent. Bothin Creek passed behind the house at the base of that slope. The report also traced earlier work: the original house dated to nineteen twenty-six, with a permitted expansion, remodeling, and creek stabilization in two thousand one. You would never recover all of that history by judging the front elevation. A property has depth, contours, water, and previous engineering decisions. Those hidden dimensions help explain why an apparently straightforward improvement can generate a substantial public planning file. This was a proposal reviewed in twenty twenty-five; the report alone does not establish what was ultimately built. But it makes a wonderful reading lesson: in Fairfax, the back of the lot may tell a very different story from the front.

spot.title: Another Household Without Another Street
spot.subtitle: The small-home idea behind ADUs

document.text: On a street like Bothin, more housing does not always have to announce itself as a new subdivision. One possibility is an accessory dwelling unit, usually called an A D U: a smaller, self-contained home associated with an existing property. ADU Marin's guide distinguishes three familiar forms. A detached cottage occupies its own little building. An attached unit shares a wall. A conversion reuses existing space, perhaps in a house or garage. Each choice rearranges the same basic ingredients: private space, shared land, utility connections, storage, and the distance between two front doors. A separate cottage can offer more privacy but takes garden space. A conversion can preserve more of the yard while inheriting the dimensions and limitations of the original structure. That is a design tradeoff, not a guarantee that a particular parcel can accommodate either option. Fairfax has its own page in ADU Marin's local guidance, and the program offers feasibility resources for working through those details. For this walk, the interesting possibility is social as much as architectural: a caregiver, an adult child, or another household can have an independent home while remaining close. A neighborhood can change one front door at a time.

spot.title: Before the Town Regulated Every Split
spot.subtitle: A small rule explains an older property map

document.text:
There is a compact piece of Fairfax history hidden in the town's subdivision code. Before incorporation in nineteen thirty-one, it says, Marin County did not regulate the division of property into three or fewer lots. The town records that it regulated all subdivisions after incorporating.

That is a useful distinction while walking among houses and fences. The neighborhood's history includes both the age of the buildings and the earlier act of creating separate parcels. Those are not necessarily the same event.

Fairfax's Historical Society dates a cluster of subdivision activity to the years before the town government existed. Bothin Park and Manor tracts came onto the market in nineteen thirteen; the Cascades followed in nineteen fourteen, with later additions. The neighborhood map was already accumulating decisions before Fairfax had its own council.

The code's historical note does not tell us how any particular property on this walk was created. It does tell us why old parcels deserve individual investigation. A modest division might have happened under different county rules from the rules later used by the town.

Imagine reading a neighborhood as two overlapping documents: the buildings people constructed and the boundaries they drew. A house can be replaced, enlarged, or remodeled while an older line persists. The street you walk through may feel like a single place, yet its property map can preserve decisions made under several different systems of government.

spot.title: Greenbrae and the Schultz Development
spot.subtitle: Local history

document.text: In nearby Greenbrae, streets were moved to make room for oak trees. Before the mid-1940s, these hills inland from Highway 101 were dairy country. Developer Niels Schultz Senior bought the property from the San Francisco Archdiocese and began building in 1946. After decades of developing neighborhoods, he wanted a community shaped around its landscape, where his own family would also live. The company rerouted streets to preserve large native trees, limited connections to Sir Francis Drake Boulevard, and dedicated planted strips along the boulevard. Those choices became part of Greenbrae’s suburban design.

Their report connected that engineering question to the public beach: holding a bluff in place can interfere with the processes that replenish sand.
